patterns.name: In-Order Sortedness
patterns.explanation: An inorder traversal of a BST produces values in sorted order. Many BST problems reduce to 'inorder traversal + check property': validate, find successor, find k-th element.
patterns.when_to_use: Validate BST (one-pass with previous value), Convert Sorted Array to BST, BST Iterator, Inorder Successor, Recover BST (two swapped nodes detected via inorder).
patterns.intuition: Inorder: left → root → right. The recursion processes the entire left subtree first, ensuring the root sees a value greater than everything before it.
common_pitfalls: Validating BST with parent-only comparison (need bounds, not just direct parent)
Failing on duplicate values (definition-dependent)
Inorder iterator not initialized correctly (must push left spine first)
Confusing inorder of BST with BFS

patterns.name: Validation with Bounds
patterns.explanation: Each node has an allowed range `(low, high)` inherited from ancestors: going left tightens `high`, going right tightens `low`. A node is valid iff its value is strictly inside its bounds.
patterns.when_to_use: Validate BST (the rigorous version), Trim BST (cut nodes outside [low, high]), Range Sum of BST, BST queries with constraints.
patterns.intuition: The BST invariant is global, not local. A node's value must beat all of its left ancestors (lower bound) and all of its right ancestors (upper bound). Bounds propagate through recursion exactly.
common_pitfalls: Comparing only with the immediate parent — fails on grandparent constraints
Using `<=` where `<` was needed (or vice versa)
Initializing bounds with `INT_MIN/INT_MAX` and overflow on edge inputs
Mixing inorder check and bounds check redundantly

patterns.name: Insert / Delete in BST
patterns.explanation: Insertion: descend until null, attach new leaf. Deletion: three cases — no child (just remove), one child (splice), two children (replace with inorder successor or predecessor and recursively delete that).
patterns.when_to_use: Insert into a Binary Search Tree, Delete Node in a BST, Trim BST. BST mutation problems.
patterns.intuition: Insertion is straightforward; deletion is hard because you must preserve the BST invariant after removing an interior node. The successor/predecessor swap reduces the two-child case to a leaf deletion.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to return the (possibly new) subtree root from the recursion
Mishandling the two-child deletion (failing to recurse on the successor's removal)
Skewing the tree into a linked list with biased input (would need balancing)
Not handling 'root deleted' (the entire tree's root may change)

patterns.name: K-th Smallest / Largest via Inorder
patterns.explanation: Inorder traversal yields sorted order; stop after K elements. With node-count augmentation per subtree, you can answer k-th in O(H) by descending: compare k to left subtree's size and recurse.
patterns.when_to_use: Kth Smallest Element in BST, Kth Largest (reverse inorder), 'with frequent inserts' variants that demand augmented BSTs.
patterns.intuition: If you know the size of the left subtree, you know whether the k-th element is on the left, at the root, or on the right. Recurse on the appropriate side with the adjusted k.
common_pitfalls: Walking the entire tree when you can short-circuit at K elements
Confusing 'k-th smallest' with 'k-th in level order'
Not maintaining subtree-size augmentation correctly under inserts/deletes
Off-by-one between 0-indexed and 1-indexed k

patterns.name: Range Queries on BST
patterns.explanation: When queries are bounded by `[low, high]`, prune subtrees: if `node.val < low`, skip the left subtree; if `node.val > high`, skip the right subtree. Otherwise visit and recurse on both.
patterns.when_to_use: Range Sum of BST, Find Mode in BST (range-bounded), counting/summing nodes in [low, high], Closest BST Value (single-value variant of bound pruning).
patterns.intuition: The BST property allows you to skip whole subtrees that can't contain values in the range. The traversal is O(H + K) where K is the number of matched nodes — much better than O(N) for narrow ranges.
common_pitfalls: Visiting all nodes anyway (correct but slow)
Inclusive vs. exclusive endpoints differ from problem to problem
Mishandling duplicates at the boundary
Confusing 'range sum' with 'k-th smallest in range' (different algorithms)
patterns.complexity_signature: O(H + K) where K = matched nodes
